incumbent.name: Tyler Johnson
incumbent.summary: Tyler Johnson, an emergency room physician from Leo, was elected in 2022 and is seeking a second term; the Senate Republican caucus lists him as assistant majority caucus chair and a member of the Education and Career Development, Elections, Family and Children Services, Health and Provider Services, and Tax and Fiscal Policy committees. {johnson_caucus}
record: 2025: Authored Senate Bill 480 on health insurers' prior authorization rules, which passed the Senate 47–2 on 2025-02-20 and took effect as Senate Enrolled Act 480 on 2025-07-01. {johnson_pa_senate} {kpc_sea480} The caucus says it sets limits on when insurers can require prior authorization, sets response deadlines and defines medically necessary care; Johnson said, "Reforming Indiana's prior authorization system has been one of my top priorities since being elected to serve in the Senate." {johnson_pa_senate}

2025-10-29: Issued a statement opposing a proposed relocation of a casino to northeast Indiana near Auburn, saying a state study "ignores risks to families, schools and public safety" and calling for an independent review of social, traffic and infrastructure costs. {johnson_casino} In 2024 he had told a New Haven town hall, "In my legislative career I've not really been for gambling." {wpta_casino}

2025-12-11: Voted for the mid-decade congressional redistricting bill, which the Senate defeated. {ipm_trump_brown} In March 2026, President Trump endorsed him among Republican senators who supported redistricting. {ipm_trump_brown}

2023–2026: The caucus lists statements on SEA 480 (2023), which addressed gender transition procedures for minors, and on SCR 17 (2023) condemning physician-assisted suicide, and a 2026 letter he co-signed with Rep. J.D. Prescott urging federal action on the abortion drug mifepristone. {johnson_caucus}

race_context: Senate District 14 covers portions of Allen and DeKalb counties in northeast Indiana. {johnson_caucus}
Johnson is the incumbent; Democrat Blaine Sefton, a union electrician, is a first-time candidate. {wboi_dems} Both were their parties' nominees after the May 5, 2026 primary. {wiki_in_senate}

Key differences in stated positions: Sefton's platform calls for repealing Senate Bill 76 (immigration enforcement), a moratorium on new data centers, and ending the private school voucher system; Johnson's record emphasizes health insurance prior authorization changes and opposition to a casino relocation in the district. {sefton_platform} {johnson_pa_senate} {johnson_casino}

candidates.summary: Blaine Sefton is a union electrician and community activist running for office for the first time. {wboi_dems}
background: Works as a union electrician and has been active with the Democratic Socialists of Fort Wayne and Indivisible Indiana, according to WBOI. {wboi_dems}

His campaign site says he is a member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers and previously worked as a case manager for the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration and at the Social Security Office of Disability Adjudication. {sefton_whoiam}
Describes himself as "a Worker, a Democratic Socialist." {sefton_site}
path_to_ballot: Filed just before the filing deadline at the start of 2026. {wboi_dems} Listed as the Democratic nominee after the May 5, 2026 primary. {wiki_in_senate}

items: Campaign platform calls for raising the minimum wage to $20.30 by 2030, supporting unionization and repealing Indiana's right-to-work law. {sefton_platform}
Proposes raising the corporate tax rate to 7.5%, incentives for small and local businesses, and a one-time 5% wealth tax on individuals worth $100 million or more. {sefton_platform}
Would bar companies and private equity firms from buying single-family homes, increase landlord accountability for repairs, and overhaul zoning rules. {sefton_platform}

Proposes a state "Medicaid-for-all" plan, requiring employers to cover medical expenses tied to their insurance plans, and reviewing nonprofit status of hospitals when patients are left with bills. {sefton_platform}
Calls for a moratorium on new data center construction, restrictions on existing centers' noise, light, water use and emissions, and an end to tax breaks for tech companies. {sefton_platform}
Supports rules, modeled on Oregon laws, making large energy users pay full cost and capping rate increases, plus building renewable generation. {sefton_platform}
Would end the private school voucher system and strengthen teachers' unions' bargaining over class size and working conditions. {sefton_platform}
Calls for repealing Senate Bill 76 and ending state cooperation with ICE, allowing sanctuary cities, repealing the abortion ban, and strengthening anti-discrimination laws. {sefton_platform}
Supports legalizing marijuana and decriminalizing low-level, nonviolent offenses. {sefton_platform}

on_incumbent: Told WBOI, "It is the responsibility of the government to work for everyday people," and said he wants to hold accountable systems he feels no longer serve people; he did not name Johnson in the material reviewed. {wboi_dems}
plans: Platform areas listed on his site: housing, health care, workers, child care, rights, data centers, taxes, roads and transit, public schools, utilities and marijuana. {sefton_platform}
Child care: cap child care costs, enact paid parental leave, and create incentives for child care workers. {sefton_platform}
endorsements_finance: His campaign site lists endorsements from the Indiana AFL-CIO, MadVoters and the Fort Wayne Democratic Socialists of America. {sefton_endorse}
gaps: Unverified (search snippet only): Transparency USA reportedly shows about $500 in contributions to his committee; no fundraising totals were verified.
Primary details (whether he had an opponent, vote count) were not verified; a Journal Gazette results snippet showed 2,375 votes but the contest was not confirmed.
A WBOI photo caption lists him in District 22 while the article text says District 14; official listings show District 14.
No statements about Tyler Johnson by name found; no positions on property taxes or redistricting found.
No debate or forum for this race found as of 2026-10-10. Little news coverage beyond one WBOI feature.

candidates.summary: Tyler Johnson is the incumbent senator, an emergency room physician from Leo first elected in 2022. {johnson_caucus}
background: Emergency room physician; the caucus lists Leo High School and the University of Saint Francis in his education. {johnson_caucus}
Serves as assistant majority caucus chair. {johnson_caucus}
path_to_ballot: Renominated in the May 5, 2026 Republican primary; Trump endorsed him in March 2026, and the Capital Chronicle described him as among senators unopposed or heavy favorites for renomination. {ipm_trump_brown} {wiki_in_senate}

items: Has said, "Too often, prior authorization stands between patients and access to the care their doctor recommends," and that SEA 480 "restores the original intent of prior authorization." {kpc_sea480}
In April 2025 issued a statement supporting the "Make Indiana Healthy Again" movement, per the caucus. {johnson_caucus}
Opposes relocating a casino to northeast Indiana near Auburn. {johnson_casino}
Voted for the 2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting bill. {ipm_trump_brown}
The caucus lists his announcements of Community Crossings road grants for the district, including about $6.1 million in March 2025 and more than $1.4 million in July 2026. {johnson_caucus}

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. No statements about Blaine Sefton were found. {johnson_caucus}
endorsements_finance: Endorsed by President Trump in March 2026. {ipm_trump_brown}
gaps: No current campaign website found (a 2022 site, votedrjohnson.us, returned 404).
His votes on the 2025 property tax law (SEA 1) and the 2025 state budget were not verified from a readable source.
No stated 2026 campaign plans or general-election statements found; no fundraising totals verified.
No debate or forum for this race found as of 2026-10-10.
